utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We apologise that it was not possible to start on time because of the competing demands on the courtroom. We come now today to a fresh witness. And before that, I understand, Mr. Petrovic, you have a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to introduce Dr. Janko Vilicic who is an expert of the Defence and one of our co-workers in the area that will be discussed today. So we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber for permission to have Dr. Vilicic present during the evidence today so that he could help us with his expertise regarding the evidence we will hear today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, has the notice of the 10th of May been filed, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have filed that. It is already filed with the Registry. If it hasn't been filed already, it will be so very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue of significance is to ensure that Dr. Vilicic is aware of the requirements as to confidentiality of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has familiarised Dr. Vilicic with this in great detail. Dr. Vilicic has taken upon himself all obligations stemming from that, and he will abide by any instructions given to him by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the circumstances, of course he may be with you in the courtroom during the evidence of relevant experts called by the Prosecution. Mr. Weiner, is it, that's going to stand?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Actually, it is both. Your Honour, thank you very much. I will turn the leading of the evidence over to Mr. Weiner, assisted by Ms. Mahindaratne, and I just wanted to let the Chamber know that I will not physically be in the courtroom during much of it but confident things will be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will miss you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's mutual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've become part of our lives. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution's next witness is Lieutenant Colonel Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be kind enough to take the card of affirmation and make the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I live in Ljubljana in the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you're employed.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I work at the centre of military schools of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've seen your resume, your background, and I just want you to comment on two points. Have you ever taught mortar targeting?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: From 1978 until 1991, I was an instructor or teacher at the artillery school in Zadar. That is where I taught controlling and directing gunfire to the cadets of the reserve officers school of the military academy and the attendees of the course for military artillery battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1991, have you taught targeting in relation to mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In 1991, I left the Yugoslav People's Army, and I got a job in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Slovenia. From 1992 until the present day, at the military schools centre of the Ministry of Defence, I have been teaching artillery rules of combat -- rules of artillery combat and rules of artillery firing. In addition to that, I teach topographic and geodesic securing of artillery mortar units, because for three years I taught military geography and military topography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Colonel, while you served in the Yugoslav People's Army, did you co-author any books in relation to artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Like any other teacher, I had the duty, like all others, to write textbooks and the like. In 1990 -- in 1985 and in 1986, a decree came from the artillery department of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army to make a new rule book of artillery firing. This was entrusted to the artillery school, namely, the department for the theory and rules of firing. I was a member of that team which worked on this -- these artillery rules of firing. We finished the draft in 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that book ever printed, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That book, I mean the rules of artillery firing, the draft, the draft was sent to units in order to have these rules checked out in practice. In 1991, this rule came back from the reviser, the proofreader, too, but I left the Yugoslav People's Army before this was printed. It was supposed to come out of print in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, can you tell us -- or tell the Court what a mortar is.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: A mortar is an artillery piece which is intended to neutralise and destroy personnel and weapons, and also to deal with the entire theatre of war as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it fire at certain angles?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The main characteristic is to use angles from 45 to 85 degrees, and that is the basic difference between a mortar and other artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you two photographs. Would you look at them. Sir, do you recognise the weapons depicted in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In these photographs, we can see an 82-millimetre mortar and a 120-millimetre mortar, M75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are those fair and accurate representations of those particular mortars, the 82- and 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer those, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many parts does a mortar consist of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- would you pause a moment. We're bringing up the relevant record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 120-millimetre mortar is P175 -- I'm sorry, P179, and the 82-millimetre mortar is P180.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many parts does a mortar consist of?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The main parts of a mortar are the barrel, the bi-pod, and its sighting equipment. Also, we should include reserve tools and equipment, although that is not an integral part of the mortar itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the base plate an integral part of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. The barrel, the bi-pod, the base plate, and the sighting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the sighting equipment. How many components does mortar sighting equipment have?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The sighting equipment roughly consists of two parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are they used for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Sighting equipment is used in order to measure the angle and of targeting and also for barrel elevation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the angle of targeting, does that refer to direction?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The angle of targeting is actually the azimuth of targeting. So this can be calculated in different ways; through mathematics and also through firing equipment, and also even through a special kind of evaluation. So basically, the direction of fire is the azimuth, and in some way we measure the angle that the gunner at the mortar will use and then target an objective, a target. When the angle is measured and when the barrel is focused on a distant point or a particular target, that means that the barrel is facing the direction of the intended target, that is to say the azimuth of targeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you're targeting for direction on azimuth, do you move the barrel from side to side or do you elevate it up and down? Strictly for direction or azimuth.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When taking an angle, that means taking the direction or azimuth. That means that it is moved left and right within a circle of 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, how do you plot the direction of a target?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When the angle for the target is calculated in some way, then that particular -- that particular angle is found on the sighting equipment, and then the barrel and the mortar are moved in order to face the pickets and to sight the pickets. At the moment when we targeted the mortar by -- vis-a-vis the pickets, that means that we have taken the right azimuth of targeting with the artillery piece itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it step-by-step. There are many parts that you just gave us. Let's begin: How do you determine the direction of the target? What's the first step you make? Do you use a map? Do you use your eyesight? Do you use binoculars? What do you use?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The azimuth of targeting can be determined in several ways; either by calculation, or graphically, or by using eyesight. Mathematically it can be calculated usually on the basis of coordinates, the coordinates of the firing position and of the target with using different patterns and also trigonometrical values of functions. Also, it is possible to use a pocket calculator with or without a programme. In artillery, for example, we used an HP25, for instance. That is one way. Another way is to handle this graphically. In order to graphically determine the azimuth of firing is to use M56, that is to say equipment for controlling and directing fire. If it is necessary, I can give a brief explanation of this. Using this equipment is actually carried out on a plancet. This is actually a piece of paper at a ratio of 1:12.500 or 1:25.000. Firing positions are marked on that as well as observation posts and the target. As for the firing position, the azimuth of the basic direction is plotted there. That is what we received from our superior officer in the orders we received. And also, there has to be a protractor in order to show the angle involved. Once we have received the target and once we've marked it on the plancet with a needle, from the firing position we lean the so-called elementary device, that is a particular device used for determining the range or distance of firing and also the angle. So once we have used this elementary device along the needle that depicts the target, and we start it from the firing position, then we can read the protractor to see what the angle for this target is. That is one of the ways in which this can be done, graphically. Another way is through a different device for firing distribution -- fire distribution. It consists of two basic elements, a base plate and also a round protractor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you're looking for that, sir, when you indicated you used a plancet, is that a grid map? Is that commonly referred to as a grid map?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: A plancet is actually a map but with a grid only, without any other elements of the map on it. So no geographical or topographical elements on it. So it's just a piece of paper, as I said, just a copy of the coordinate system or grid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you turn the --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I can show this here, perhaps, on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That is the snopar for determining targets of -- elements of targeting. That is the piece of equipment that is used for fire distribution. It can be used together with a map but it can also be used without a map. The procedures for determining elements of targeting can differ to a certain extent. When a map is used, we plot the firing position, the observation post, and the target. We use a line to bring together the firing position and the target in the following way: The length would have to exceed by 2 or 3 centimetres the disk involved. You see the circle here? That is the disk. So this other part is the base. When we use a map and this device, then we also use the disk. Of course the disk has to be prepared for determining the elements for targeting. I'm going back to the map now. So on the map I have a firing position, an observation post, and the target, and I have this line that links the two together, the firing position and the target. Then there is the disk, which I put with its centre on the firing position, the centre of the firing position. So this is the basic thing that a mortar unit uses, regardless of whether it's a platoon or a company or whatever. We put the disk north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, rather than describe this for the record, I'll get a photocopy of it at the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you use these two methods, whether it's the protractor or this snopar method, and you get an angle, you indicated that you then turn the mortar towards a post or a pole. Are you talking about surveyor's poles, surveyor poles, those white poles that surveyors use in the streets? That type of a pole?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Well, we call them pickets. It's a pole. It's a piece of wood in red and white which is placed in front or behind the mortar, thereby marking the main direction according to which later we take a particular angle with the weapon. So it's very similar to the equipment used by -- by geodesic experts. So -- but they also have a board which they use, whereas we only use this picket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, once you adjust the mortar, the mortar direction to a certain angle based on using that pole, do you then determine the distance, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The angle and the distance are approximately determined at the same time, so conditionally we can say that first of all we determine the angle and then the distance. So once the angle is determined, then we go about establishing the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you establish the distance, which way do you move the barrel? The barrel of the mortar, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When we determine the distance of firing from the firing tables and then we read what the distance is, then we see from there what the elevation is and then, in that example, the mortar is moved according to height. So based on the distance based on which we determined the elevation, the mortar and the barrel are moved by height. A certain elevation is set and taken in order to hit the actual target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you determine the distance, do you have to use any charts to calculate the degrees that you moved that mortar up and down, the degrees that you elevate the barrel of the mortar? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The distance of the firing, in principle, is determined in the same way as we determine the angle. It can be calculated. It can be done graphically, or when it's not possible to do it in any other way it's just done by visual methods. So once you determine the distance in one of these three ways, then you take the firing tables, and based on the firing tables, you choose additional charges. And after that, you read from the firing tables the elevation which should be -- or the range finder, which should be taken by the sighting or by the section of the sighting or piece of it which we call the range finder. When we take the right range and the right elevation, then we raise the barrel or lower the barrel for -- until the cross-hairs match on the sighting. When the horizontal and the vertical cross-hairs are in a position that they should be in, then the barrel is in the appropriate elevation which corresponds to a certain firing distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I just want to go over something quick. You indicated that you can determine distance visually, you can determine it by the use of maps. In 1991, were laser range finders used by the JNA to determine distance?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Laser range finders were used before 1991. They were used from the 1980s, perhaps even a year or so before that. I came to Zadar in 1978, and we were using laser range finders then. So from the 1980s onwards, that is part of the normal equipment that was used, used in order to measure the distance to the target from the observation points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to cover one more factor of targeting. Can weather be a factor in targeting or changing one's targets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As we know, firing tables take into account certain firing conditions. Actual firing in itself is never actually carried out in precisely those conditions which are stated in the firing tables. For initial elements of firing to be as precise as possible, it is necessary to calculate the meteorological and the ballistic corrections which correspond to the conditions in which the actual firing is taking place. So we would take into account the atmospheric conditions which do have an effect on the precision of firing. So if possible, they should be calculated into the general calculation as well as the topographical elements which are created based on topographical firing elements. Then these elements are corrected and meteorological and ballistic firing conditions are calculated into those elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which meteorological or weather factors do you consider?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: With a mortar, we take the azimuth into consideration as well as the wind speed, also the temperature of the air and the pressure. As far as ballistic conditions are concerned, which we also have to take into account, that would be the initial velocity and the temperature of the gunpowder or the temperature of the charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the JNA are artillery officers or mortar officers trained to consider meteorological factors or weather factors?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As I said, I taught artillery rules of firing and theory of artillery firing for 13 years, and in all that time, we had cadets from military schools, from the military academy, the school for reserve officers, and even at the commanders' training courses, whom we taught to calculate the meteorological and ballistic conditions. I believe that as soon as they -- once they had completed all of these military training schools, that they had received their training in all of these subjects as well, otherwise they would not have completed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the JNA in 1991 have a section which provided weather information?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In order to determine the meteorological conditions of firing, we had meteorological stations in the artillery department, and those stations, with the help of meteorological balloons, which was out in the field, which had a radar at the end, determined the meteorological conditions for firing, and they transmitted this to all units, the meteorological data, in the form of a meteorological bulletin, on a separate channel and frequency at predetermined times, which was always stated in orders, commands, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this exist in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's move on to page 13 of your report where you talk about distribution of fire. What is distribution of fire? What does it concern?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The distribution of fire on the target is achieved by choosing the correct beam for the depth of the target, determining the direction in which the target stretches, setting the beam, and echeloning the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the word "cluster." What is the cluster? I think they're translating it as the word "beam."

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The cluster, snop, according to the military lexicon, is the distribution of weapons on the firing position through which you achieve an equal distribution of impact or hits on the target. That would be the simplest definition of a cluster, snop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a snop, a cluster along the width of a target?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Targets up to 100 metres wide are fired at with a concentrated cluster, meaning that all the barrels, all the firing azimuths from all of the weapons are looking at the same point, the centre of the target, namely. If the target is broader than 100 metres, then a cluster is determined along the width of the target. So besides determining the cluster, you would also establish the direction that the target goes along in order to carry out corrections in order to coordinate or get a more precise cluster, in order to get a more precise target coverage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to make this easier, I'll give you a few sheets of paper, and why don't you draw a concentrated cluster and a cluster along the width of the targets so the Court can see what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: So let's assume that these are four mortars, and assume that this is a target up to 100 by 100 metres. The centre of the target is marked with the letter C. Such a target is fired at with a concentrated cluster, meaning that all the trajectories are directed to one point. If the width of the target is greater than 100 metres, and if we assume that the target is at an angle in relation to the weapons, such a target is hit with a cluster spread along the width of the target, meaning that each weapon has its own sector of the target. So that is actually how we direct the cluster along the width of the target. We do this by calculating the corrections, because there is no point in moving the mortars themselves in order to receive or to get a correct distribution of the hits. With the assistance of the earlier-mentioned plotting circle, we make sure that each weapon is corrected for their own area, and this is later checked through a range correction board, and then each weapon targets its own picket, or pole, and then it will focus on that section of the target that it is supposed to fire at, which the shell is supposed to hit, whereby we secure the proper distribution of fire along the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you put a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you put an A over the concentrated target.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: A concentrated beam or a cluster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. And a B over the one over the width of the target, which you've already done. Could you date that and sign that, sir, on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I'd like to offer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P181.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, could you continue with a piece of paper. Could you tell us what is the effective zone of fire? What is the effective zone of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Each projectile has its own effective zone of fire which, first of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all, depends on the calibre, on the type of the projectile. The type of the projectile if we're thinking of the calibre but also of the type, whether we're talking about a mortar or an artillery projectile. So this effective zone of fire tells us that in that section the target will be neutralised in any case to a certain degree. The place of impact -- if the place of impact is closer, the probability is greater that the target will be destroyed. And then as we move towards the outside, the probability of the target being hit decreases. For example, for a 120-millimetre mortar, the effective zone is 60 metres, meaning that within that area the target will be damaged to a certain degree and neutralised to a certain degree. It's possible that it will be completely neutralised or disabled or it will be -- it will suffer some minor damage. These are the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, group fire, can you just briefly tell us what that is, group fire. You mention it in a sentence or so in your report. Could you briefly explain that.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We call that group firing. So group fire is one of the three stages, or the third stage of artillery firing in which, following the preparation of initial elements and after the completion of corrections during the transfer of fire, we fire a certain calculated or approved quantity of projectiles and achieve the material or moral effect on the target. That would be the simplest definition of group fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be basically once you've honed in on your target you fire a number of shells on it? Everyone starts firing on it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: After preparation is completed, as well as the correction during the transfer of fire, then the average trajectory goes through the centre of the target and a certain quantity of ammunition is fired at that target in order to exert a material and moral effect on the target or to achieve some degree of neutralisation of the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also mention one more term, "echeloning of fire," and can you just tell us briefly what that means, echeloning of fire.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Echeloning of fire or of shots is firing of targets which are at a greater depth, targets which are up to a depth of 200 metres with the changes in the range finder, meaning that we hit a target generally at three ranges. This is mostly used on targets which have a depth from 100 to 200 metres. If they're deeper than 200 metres, the effect of echeloning of fire is very slight, and generally such a target is treated as two separate targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's move to expenditure norms. What are expenditure norms?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Expenditure norms are quantities of ammunition that most probably will secure a certain effect on the target. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is neutralisation in relation to expenditure norms?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Rules of firing gives tables of ammunition expenditure, and these tables are drafted based on some basic parameters or elements, and these tables were drafted for the 25 per cent level of neutralisation. They were made for the width of a target of one hectare or 100 metres. They were also drafted for firing elements during complete preparation for impact, or immediate impact, and also for firing to a distance of up to ten kilometres. I can say that with artillery fire, you can achieve several tasks; one is neutralisation, second is destruction, and the third we could say, and I'm talking about the basic tasks, would be disruption. Then we also have smoke curtains and also illumination. Disruption would be a neutralisation percentage of up to 10 per cent. Neutralisation constitutes a term ranging from 10 to 50 per cent. A target is destroyed or considered to be destroyed if the degree of neutralisation is greater than 50 per cent. So what level or degree of neutralisation depends on our assignment. First of all, it depends on the task which was given to the artillery or mortar units by their superior commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as we speak about neutralisation, could you please look at the tables on page 15, the bottom of page 15, running into page 16 of your report. The heading is Fire Task, Type and Characteristics of Target, and Normative Unit. The first column, parts 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, those all concern neutralisation on unobserved targets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes; 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. That table pertains to neutralisation of unobserved targets, although practically we do know what the type of target is but we don't know how big it is and we don't know its exact position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next three numbers, 7, 8, and 9, concern neutralisation 25 per cent of observed targets over one hectare.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That part of the table under 7, 8, 9, gives the expenditure norms of projectiles or, rather, ammunition for neutralising a target of one hectare, the degree of neutralisation 25 per cent, and that would be an observed target, namely, one that can be seen from the observation post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want to look on the top of page 16, 4D, "a platoon (battery) of weapons in the open," there's a 90 to the right. Does that mean that to neutralise 25 per cent of a platoon battery of weapons in the open you would need 90 projectiles? So mortars would have to fire 90 projectiles to neutralise that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If you're referring to item number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to. And for the record, one hectare is what amount of space?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: One hectare is 100 metres by 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to direct and indirect fire. It's mentioned on page 8 of your report. You describe both direct and indirect fire. My question to you is: Which is more effective in targeting; direct or indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: At any rate, direct fire is more effective than indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: First of all, in the case of direct fire, the dispersion is considerably less than in the case of indirect fire. You can see the target. You can affect targeting itself. You do not have any intermediary. When you have a direct -- when you have direct firing, then you quite simply see your target. You see it from where the weapon is, and that is certainly far simpler than indirect firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of weapons did the JNA use, according to your study, in the Dubrovnik area that are direct-fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As far as I know about the materials that deal with the attacks on Dubrovnik, in principle what was used was the Maljutka anti-armour rocket when we are talking about weapons for direct firing, that is. The Maljutka 911, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are recoilless cannons, tanks, and anti-aircraft [Realtime transcript read in error "aircraft"] weapons, are they direct fire or indirect fire weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Tanks, recoilless weapons [as interpreted] are all weapons for direct fire, yes. In that example, I mentioned first and foremost anti-armour rockets, 911s, because in the reports on operations against Dubrovnik that were established both by the commission of the Yugoslav Army and the UNESCO commission and that of the government of the Republic of Croatia, most of the hits, or perhaps even all the hits that were directly fired were primarily from rockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two corrections, Your Honour, for the transcript. On page 20, line 3, it says "aircraft weapons." That should be anti-aircraft. And on line 5, it says "tanks, recoilless weapons." That should be recoilless cannons. That's what was said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what type of weapons were used by the JNA that are indirect fire-type weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: According to these same reports that I have already mentioned, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting the witness, Your Honour, and my learned friend, but in order to be as clear Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as possible, could we please hear what reports the witness is actually referring to? The witness mentioned two reports. I'm just guessing which ones he's referring to, but could this please be clarified for us what reports the witness means when referring to these two reports because it cannot be seen clearly from the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you follow that up, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said reports. You indicated previously a number of reports. One was the commission of the Yugoslav Army, the UNESCO commission, and the one of the Republic of Croatia. Are those the reports that you're referring to again?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: On the 8th of December, 1991, a commission of the Yugoslav Army, the Yugoslav People's Army, together with the top people of the town of Dubrovnik compiled a report. That's the first report. The second report, if I'm not mistaken, was done on the 10th of December. The representatives of UNESCO and the representatives of the government of the Republic of Croatia also compiled a report concerning operations against Dubrovnik. When I mentioned them the first time and the second time, those were the reports that I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, what sort of weapons were used that constitute indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: 82-millimetre mortars were used and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what sort of targets do you use direct fire for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As a rule, direct fire is used for very important targets, for individual targets, for all those targets that we can see from the firing position where the weapon actually is. As I've already pointed out, direct fire is more effective than indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of targets would you use indirect fire for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We use indirect fire for those targets that we cannot target directly, those that are covered, and also by weapons that are covered. When the weapons used for indirect firing and the targets are covered, that is to say when the targets cannot be seen and also when the firing positions and the weapons themselves cannot be seen. So as a rule, they are on the surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just one last portion on direct fire, one last matter. When you usually fire a tank or a recoilless cannon, you aim and fire. With a Maljutka, can you continue to direct the rocket or the missile after it's fired?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not receiving any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat that answer. It wasn't translated into English. Sorry. The question was: When you usually fire a tank or a recoilless cannon, you aim and fire. With a Maljutka, can you continue to direct the rocket or missile towards its target? And could you please repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Maljutka or, rather, the 911 anti-armour rocket is a guided projectile, and it can be guided almost throughout the flight, and the flight can be affected practically throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we taking the break at the usual time today, or since we started about 20, 25 minutes late, do we continue until about 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have no fixed view, but I thought we'd run on for about ten minutes. Just one moment, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears, Mr. Weiner, we're asked to have a break at the normal time, and more than that, there is a failure in the equipment cooling system for the electronics, which means that we must move courtroom, and we need to break at the normal time because the equipment is overheating and we don't want to put it at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid it means we move to Courtroom II. Do you want to go on for a minute or two or is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to start on a new subject, so I think it's probably a convenient time to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am sorry for the inconvenience of the move. Most of you have managed better than the Bench. We have not yet received our papers, but we will carry on nevertheless. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have extra diagram paper if the Court would like to use it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have extra diagram paper for the witness if the Court would like to make use of some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Poje, we're going to start a new subject, working maps for headquarters. Are you familiar with those types of maps?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what those maps are?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Working maps are maps in which the decisions of commanders and commanding officers are marked, and they are used to provide the units with instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do these maps depict the positions of the armies?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The deployment of units is depicted in such maps. It would be hard to say that the unit is located at a particular point, but the map shows an area where a unit is or where its firing positions are or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Because, practically, only after reconnaissance the exact location of a unit can be established or, rather, where the basic weapon will be for an artillery battery, where an observation post will be, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the units are deployed. Does that include the weaponry? Do these maps depict weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Maps usually depict units, and those weapons that are of crucial importance for the activity of the unit itself. That is how a mortar platoon is depicted, a mortar battery, and so on, even a squad at a position, a platoon at a position, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these maps reliable --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these maps reliable, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, they are, because these maps are used for command and control of units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would they be omitting positions on these maps?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Probably there wouldn't be any units that would not be depicted. Perhaps it could only happen that a unit would be depicted in one particular place and then later, upon reconnaissance, it is in another position, and that particular location had not been observed yet and therefore not depicted on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do they use symbols on these maps?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Every unit is marked individually and weapons are marked with their own symbols. These symbols are part of the instructions for charting working maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the -- do the maps or the symbols on the maps indicate the exact location of a weapon or the units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Maps, as a rule, show areas of deployment. So I would say an approximation. We have to know that plans of operations are made in headquarters, and there is still the possibility of a change, smaller or bigger, of the position itself. So what is depicted on the map Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. practically is the area where the unit is supposed to take its position, and it is the X and Y axis that show this location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to show you three maps; P132, P159, and P160. I would just like you to look at these maps and tell us if you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I do recognise these maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen these maps previously?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you use these maps in preparing your report in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When I wrote my report, I did use these maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us start with map P159. Sir -- Colonel, take a look at it for a moment. There have been three modifications to that map based on witness testimony. The rocket artillery position in square A is instead in the position of circle A. Do you see that? Could you speak a little louder, sir, so the recorder --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second change is the mortar position in a square marked B was not in deployment on 6 December 1991, according to Witness Negodic. And then finally, the ZIS cannon in a square marked C is now in a position at circle C. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming these three modifications, does it change your opinion as to who or which side did or did not fire into the Old Town on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This new situation does not change the actual state of affairs. Practically what happened was just some unit movement but not major unit movement, not anything that would affect combat activity in any major way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, we will get back to map 159 a little bit later. Could you please move to map 160, 160. Map 160 possesses those same three modifications found on map 159, the map you just saw, and in addition to that, it has a Maljutka position marked D, D in a circle. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the other three changes; A, B, and C?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, B, C, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do these four changes on this map, does it change your opinion as to who or which side did or did not fire into the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: All of those changes do not change the report that I submitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the basis of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Same as I've already said: They do not substantially affect the combat operations around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to the maps in a little while. Sir, I just want to ask you a question based on the transcript. I asked you if you saw changes A, B, and C, and you said, "Yes, B, C, I do." Did you also see change A on that second map?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: There are no changes under A on that map, or I'm not seeing it. B, C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see circle A on that map -- cross A.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And again, just for the record, does that make -- does that change your conclusion, those modifications?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No, it does not change the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. What I'd like to do is move to accuracy for a while, and we'll get back to the maps after we talk about accuracy. When you fire a large number of projectiles and the conditions are basically the same, will they land or impact in the same spot, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Due to accidental errors, even though we say that a large number of projectiles fired under the same conditions is carried out, those projectiles will not hit exactly the same point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, if you fired two projectiles, would those two land --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to the transcript, the witness said they will not hit one point but they will hit one area, and that is not in the transcript. That is page 5, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you fire two projectiles with all conditions being the same, will they land in the same spot?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't they land in the same spot or same point?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Although it seems to us that the firing conditions are the same, those two projectiles were not actually fired under the same conditions. This happens because of errors which accompany each firing. These are errors on which we do not have any -- which we do not have any influence on and which are a part of each firing, and not only of each firing but also of each measuring process, and that is why two projectiles, even though they "are fired under equal conditions" will fall on two different points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, if you ask -- if you fire a large number of projectiles, will they land in the same spot?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we fire a large number of projectiles, and if we -- well, those projectiles will not have the same trajectory. There will be a cluster of trajectories, and if that cluster of trajectories is severed by a vertical line and we watch the place where the projectiles will hit, we will then have an area which those projectiles will strike, and we will also have their trajectories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, is there a name for this area or for this shape in which the projectiles disperse?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: We call that dispersion, and this dispersion is in the shape of an ellipsis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could give you a few sheets of paper and move a few of the maps, I'd ask you to do a few diagrams for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO so the Court could see, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you draw an ellipse for us. Could you please do that.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that dispersion is characterised by an individual ellipse. The axes, semi-axes of this ellipse we will mark with the letters Vd and Vp. So these would be deviations by length or distance and by direction. So these are semi-axes of the individual dispersion ellipse. The pattern of dispersion, theoretically, is infinite, practically, so that it can range from plus/minus 4 Vd times plus/minus 4 Vp. That is the practical picture of impact dispersion, which is a result of unintentional errors while firing. And these unintentional errors are errors over which we can have no influence. We can, for example, have just the interval between the first and the second shell or the imperfection of the senses of the person who is doing the measurements, for example, the targeting elements and so on. There is also the built-in tolerance in the equipment or apparatus that is being used. So this entire picture of impact dispersion ranges from plus/minus 4 Vd and plus/minus 4 Vp. The centre of the dispersion ellipse is the intersection between those two dispersion axes. So then we would get an average trajectory in order to get an average point of impact. So now we are looking at 1, 2, 3, 4, and 1, 2, 3, 4 -- 1, 2, 3 like this. So this is what this dispersion pattern would look like. The probability of dispersion in one direction or the other direction, closer or further from the centre of dispersion, or to the left or to the right, is practically equal. The closer we are to the average impact, the probability is greater that we will actually hit the target, because the whole zone of impact of the projectiles is from the edges towards the centre, and as it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. moves more from the edges to the centre, the density of impacts grows, is greater and greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few things as we go along. The vertical line running through from top to bottom, is that the Vd line? Is that Vd?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That is Vd, and that is also the direction -- this is the dispersion axis in the direction of fire. And this is Vp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is the horizontal line; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This is by the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have four sections. Do you establish concentric ellipses within these four sections when you determine the error, factor the error of dispersion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: There are four ellipses, and the probability of the projectile falling inside one of those ellipses is different. The distribution of impact could be also presented in that way. We could have an average point of impact -- We will just take one direction by distance. That is Vd. The probability of a projectile deviating to the left or to the right by 1 Vd point is 25 per cent. From 1 Vd to 2 Vd, the probability is 16 per cent. From 2 to 3 Vd it's 7 per cent, and from 3 to 4, it's 2 per cent. Meaning if we're looking at a half of the ellipse, it's 50 per cent. In the same way, it would be 16, 7, and 2 on the other side, away from us. So that would also be 50 per cent. So the total probability, the practical probability that the projectiles will hit within those perimeters is 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, can you take those same percentages, the 25, 16, 7, and 2, and place them in the concentric ellipses? Can that be done in determining probabilities?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Practically, the diagram that I made in a straight line actually corresponds to the ellipse, because the inside part, the inside ellipse is coverage by 50 per cent and so on and so forth. So to the left and to the right, the percentage is 25 per cent. To the left would be 25 per cent, then 16, 7, and 2 on this side within the ellipse, and then also to the other side would be the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you place the 25 per cent in the ellipse or in the half of the ellipse.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Exactly 25 per cent if we look at it from whatever side. It's 25 per cent if we're viewing it from the aspect of the direction. Or if we look at each of the quadrants that I drew, then the percentage is 6.25 per cent. The probability of a projectile landing in that quadrant would be 6.25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you get closer to the centre, because you're dealing with the higher numbers, would the -- would the density of impacts be higher?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think I already said that, but I will say it again. From the periphery of the dispersion ellipse towards the centre, the concentration of impacts is higher and higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I just want to clarify for the record again. The line going vertically from top to bottom, is that the Vd line on the ellipse? The line going from top to bottom, vertically.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That line shown on this diagram, which at the same time is the line of firing, actually is Vd. The semi-axis perpendicular to that is Vd [as interpreted] and that is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The horizontal line that runs through the middle from left to right, that's Vp; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Vd refers to the distance or the range?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Vd is on the firing-line, yes, on the firing-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Vp refers to the deflection?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Deflection in the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you took the whole interior of that first concentric circle, would that be 50 per cent -- the area where 50 per cent of the projectiles would impact, the whole concentric circle, not just the semi-ellipse?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: 50 per cent would impact that section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The second part would have a 16 per cent impact rate. The third ellipse would have an impact percentage of 7, and the last outer ellipse would have a 2 percentage impact rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But if you took the whole ellipse, the 16 is one-half, the whole ellipse would be 32, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The area of all of the four ellipses can -- will have 100 per cent of the fired projectiles fall into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the centre one has 30 -- I'm sorry, has 50 per cent, the outside one, the second one, would have 32 per cent, 16 plus 16?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third ellipse would have 7 plus 7 for 14?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Fourteen. And the last one would have 4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four. Okay. Now, when you're determining these ellipses, does distance affect the area of dispersion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Changing the firing distance would change the dispersion pattern according to direction and according to distance. The greater the firing distance, the greater the dispersion pattern, in principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the use of a charge? If you change the type of charge, will that affect the dispersion, be it one charge or several charges being used?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we're using the same firing distance and change the charge or the additional charge of the mortar, then the dispersion pattern will also change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're trying to place -- when you're trying to use a charge or determine how many charges to use, what is your goal in relation to dispersion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: One of the elements on which the charge choice depends -- well, the first element is the firing distance. The second is the dispersion. You choose practically that charge which in the given firing conditions at that distance provides for the smallest dispersion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you mean by that that you want the charge that would send the most projectiles into the target area?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That would come as close as possible to the targets, because we said that not all projectiles will hit the targets if we take that the target is the average of the projectiles that hit it, then we would choose our charges with a smaller dispersion pattern, meaning that we achieve a greater concentration over a smaller area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these ellipses that you've provided in your addendum and the ones that you're talking about now, do they take into effect error factors other than the dispersion error factors, such as miscalculations, equipment malfunction? Do your ellipses take those matters into account?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I've already said that the dispersion pattern is the result of accidental errors. I tried to mention some of them, the imperfection of the senses, the rounding up of elements, and some imperfections in the measuring equipment, in the shells, in the mortars, even a change in the firing conditions from one projectile to the next. So all of these things would affect the dispersion pattern. For example, the introduction of modern guiding and control firing systems, the introduction of more advanced guiding systems would reduce the dispersion area. It's not possible to avoid dispersion, but it's possible to reduce it. For example, we used to use a stereoscopic range finder with a large margin of error, but then we introduced a laser range finder which really does reduce measuring errors so that -- and an error would also be possible depending on the instrument gauge and the degree to which the gauge measurements were rounded off to. So it depends on what the requirements were of the person actually using those measuring apparatus. So there were ways to reduce overall levels in order to achieve a small -- the smallest dispersion possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get away from dispersion just for a few moments and then come right back to it. I want to talk about your dispersion charts in the addendum. You mention -- or in your different examples you use charges -- or you use shells, M74, M75, M62P3. Why did you use those shells throughout your examples or hypotheticals?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: When I was making the calculation for the dispersion patterns in different cases, depending on the firing position and the position of the target, I used the ordinary ammunition, ammunition which is used most commonly. Had I taken other types of ammunition, I would not have come to significantly different results. Secondly, when I was calculating all of this, I've already said that you can choose the type of charge. At certain firing distances, it is also possible to use several charges, third, fourth, or fifth charges. So I also tried to figure out the dispersion in this first, second, or third case. I don't know exactly which charges were used in the specific examples that we're dealing with, so I tried to present the theories that changing a charge over a same distance would change the dispersion pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your hypotheticals you also use pretty much the same fuses. Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: A fuse does not actually have any major effect on the dispersion pattern. Well, each change does have an effect on the dispersion pattern, but fuses do not have a significant effect because the fuses do not really differentiate substantially from one to the other, and they do not have a substantial effect on the dispersion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there are two shells that you didn't mention, and I just want to ask you just quickly about them. Speaking of the types of shells, are flares or smoke shells fired by mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Mortars which are used to create smokescreens would use smoke shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about smoke shells. Are smoke shells commonly used by mortar units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Smoke shells are used by those units which have such projectiles in their combat kits. Smoke shells are used in order to create smokescreens in order to prevent observation and combat operations of the enemy. Smokescreens are also used in order to pull out your own unit under cover from the position. Smoke shells are also used in order to illuminate or indicate where the target is. So these are the main purposes of using smoke shells: To disable the enemy, prevent him from operating, and to enable your own unit, the unit that is being supported, to pull back from its position. That would be -- those would be main objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are smoke shells generally found in the combat kits?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In combat kits, smoke shells can also be found. There are some, as well as flares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that smoke shells can also be used for illumination. Do they contain any substances that you're aware of, smoke shells, such as phosphorous? Do you know whether smoke shells contain phosphorous?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Correction. Smoke shells are not used for illuminating targets but for creating smokescreens. An integral part of a smoke shell is white phosphorous, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any problem with smoke shells causing fire because of their containing phosphorous?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Easily inflammable materials can be lit in this way. We had many such examples in the open where, due to smokescreens, there were fires. First of all it was dried grass that went on fire. A smoke shell burns even under water, that is to say, in the water. So we could say that in the case of easily inflammable materials, this would invariably happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you include wood as an easily flammable material?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. What I'd like to do is to move on to your addendum, and specifically to page 4. There's a chart on page 4 under Question 11 c). It concerns a 120-millimetre mortar firing from Zarkovica. Page 4 in the English. Concerns a 120-millimetre mortar, and then also an 82-millimetre mortar firing from Zarkovica into Ploce. Could you, first, looking at the 120-millimetre chart, please explain it. Could you please explain to the Court what the chart means, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The first example that was dealt with here is the firing position at Zarkovica of the 120-millimetre mortar. The target is Ploce. The firing range is 2.300 metres. I took this example of using third, fourth, or fifth charge for targeting that particular target. As for the third charge, for instance, in the firing tables for the third charge, in column -- columns 11 and 12 -- so we look at the third charge. That's the 3. The firing range is 2.300 metres. And in column 11 and in column 12, as opposed to the range, we see the magnitude of the probable deviation. 11 is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: -- the -- 12 is the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what 11 and 12 are, please. Could you point it out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Column 11 and column 12 in all tables of firing that the Yugoslav People's Army used for artillery and mortar units contain Vd and Vp. First and foremost, in order to avoid errors when weapons are changed. For example, if you move from a 105 to a mortar, the Vd and the Vp would always have to be in columns 11 and 12. Like all the other relevant figures, they would have to be under the same column. The figures would have to be in the same places simply in order to have this done uniformly. And I said what the reason was. So that even if a weapon is changed, there would not be any confusion or some other kind of possible mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, one moment, please. Colonel, you're referring to mortar targeting tables. Could you first identify the book that you're referring to for the Court. Could you identify the front cover of the book, please, on the targeting tables. And could you read the -- read the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: "Firing Tables for the Light Mortar of 120 millimetres, M75."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The edition of 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that same edition used in 1991 by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you first show us the tables and explain what those are, take us from each of the columns so we understand that.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If I go back to the third charge that we have already mentioned, we can see that in column number 1 the distance or, rather, range is marked, that is to say from the firing position to the target. Column number 2 is finder -- is the range finder, 1 to 6.000. So the circle is divided into 6.000 sections. Then column number 3. It says the angle, but we can also say elevation. Again, 1 to 6.000. In column number 4 is this same elevation or this same angle which corresponds to the distance or range in terms of degrees or minutes. Column 6 -- under number 6, that is, talks about the highest point of the trajectory, that is to say the highest point that the shell reaches along its trajectory. Column 7 refers to the time of flight of the projectile. It is important not to have to look through the instruments all the time and to wait for 35 or 40 seconds until the shell actually lands. Column number 9 refers to the angle of descent, that is to say the angle under which the shell falls. And we've already referred to columns 11 and 12. That is Vd in 11 and Vp in 12. So range error probable, and deflection error probable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the 3 in the middle of the page that's in a different colour, that's in blue as opposed to the black numbers in the columns, does that refer to the charge being used, charge 3?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That number 3 implies the number of additional charges. So it is the third charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these tables that you're using, have you commonly used these tables for your training and for the thousands of mortar shells that you've fired?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are these necessary? Are tables necessary for targeting and firing mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In the 1980s, some changes took place in the firing tables, because until then, we could use the so-called ballistics for such information. This is a type of graphic firing table that we used, and you could directly read what the elevation should be in terms of the range. You could also read the time of flight required. In the 1980s, some materials were changed, and therefore new firing tables were made. While I was in the army, there weren't any new ones, so we used the firing tables for determining, for example, the range, the distance. We use it just as I used it here in order to establish the dispersion pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now to the right on this next page there are several other columns. Are those also important to your calculations?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: These columns contain table corrections. When we talked about meteorological and ballistic conditions of firing and the necessity to calculate meteorological corrections in order to establish actual corrections, then these columns are used, the ones on the other page of the firing tables, all the way up to column 1 again. Can we see it here? Column 18, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, and again we go back to column 1. So these are the table corrections, and we use them to multiply the deviation of the actual conditions in respect of the values provided for in the firing tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell us what pages those two tables fall in that book so we can photocopy them at the break? If you can just leave the book here, we can -- you've mentioned that book in your footnote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, getting back to our original chart on page 4 of your addendum, you showed us where you got the V -- the Vd and the Vp. Could you finish explaining what this table means.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we look at this firing table and if we look at this firing range of 2.300 metres, we have read the Vd values, 14 metres, and the probable deviation would be 10 metres. These are semi-axes of dispersion ellipses. We said that the entire dispersion pattern contains plus/minus 4 Vd, that is to say 8 Vd, and plus/minus 4 Vp, that is to say 8 Vp. And in this table that I prepared here, I wrote out the semi-axis of the dispersion ellipses, 4 times 14 because of plus/minus 56 metres. These are the semi-axes of dispersion ellipses. So 1 is 56 metres. Also, in terms of direction, 10 is the semi-axis of -- so then there is 40 metres. The semi-axis is 40. So this is the entire dispersion pattern. If we look at it now, we see the range, 112 metres. And in terms of direction, the dispersion is 80 metres. So that is the dispersion pattern under given conditions of targeting or firing. Or the most probable dispersion pattern. Perhaps I should put it that way. It was calculated for the fourth and for the fifth charge as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I just want to get this correct. You start off with the 14 Vd, and each of those four sections that you showed us, you have the ellipse and there's four ellipses, four sections. Each of those are 14 metres long, for a total of 56 metres? Yes. And horizontally, each one of those are ten metres wide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So half the ellipse is 56 by 40, and the whole ellipse is double that, 112 metres by 80 metres?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we consider the semi-axis of dispersion the top half of the ellipse, the part which is farthest away from those firing and closest to the Old Town, that would be the 56 by 40, the top part of it, would any part of that ellipse enter or overlap into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As far as I know, taking into account the position of the targets, the possible targets that were engaged, not a single one of the calculated ellipses does not go into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about the one -- the one with charge 3, but as you said, all six of them, 120-millimetre mortar, charges 3, 4, and 5, and the 82-millimetre mortar, charges 3, 4, and 5. You indicated not one of the semi-ellipses mentioned in that addendum on page 4, not one of them would enter or overlap into the Old Town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there are additional hypotheticals on pages 5 through 9, firing from Zarkovica, target Bogosica Park on page 5. Then on the bottom of page 5 into 6, firing from Zarkovica towards Srdj; and then firing position Bosanka, target Ploce, and that's the Lazareti example, from Bosanka to Lazareti or Ploce. And below that is from Bosanka targeting Bogosica Park. And finally -- there are a few more. From Bosanka targeting Srdj, on pages 7 and 8. And on pages 8 and 9, Srdj targeting Ploce and Srdj targeting Bogosica Park. Based on your calculations relating to the JNA mortars firing from those positions, do any of the semi-axes of the dispersion ellipses in those calculations overlap or enter the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Not a single semi-axis of dispersion touches town or goes into town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the JNA was firing from any of those positions at any of those stated targets, none of these shells would disperse into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: As for these examples that I calculated and the ones that were referred to just now, the semi-axes of the dispersion ellipses are less than 100 metres. That means that practically it was impossible for any one of the dispersion patterns to involve the town, neither a single part nor its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Poje, utilising these calculations and these tables, would any of the dispersion strike the walls of the Old Town? Basically, would any of these semi-axes of the dispersion ellipses overlap with the walls of the Old Town? Not just enter the Old Town but overlap the walls on these, the pages 5 through 9 as well as the one on page 4. So the ones on pages 4 through 9.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In all these calculations, that is to say these three firing positions and three targets, not in a single one -- so actually, the targets are more far away than the dispersion pattern. So not a single dispersion pattern touches upon the Old Town, let alone enter it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, did you calculate some hypothetical situations where JNA mortars are firing at Croatian anti-aircraft guns, what the projectile dispersion would be in relation to the Old Town? Did you calculate any of these hypotheticals in your supplements?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
